title: Change in boat music from ragtime to saxophone arrangements
summary: Mason explains how adding saxophones changed the music and arranging, crediting Don Redman with new harmonies.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Well did you play, you said you played mostly dance tunes, but did you play, you played some ragtime on the boat?

Oh yes, well on the boat, when we first started, of course the music, the music on the boat changed, you see, from the jazz music, from what they call ragtime, because when we, after we got them saxophones, of course we changed the whole, after they switched from where they had the trumpets, plainly, to where they had the saxophones, the whole style of music changed. As a matter of fact, the whole style of writing music changed. You see, when, if I can remember rightly, I think the first, the first, first of the music in the popular, in popular form where they started using augmented chords and all that stuff, double augmented chords and began to bring what they, bring music, what you call up to, away from where it was just playing this four, and this four, four and over chord where they had to spread the chords out, where you brought seventh and ninth and broken, fifth and broken, ninth and all that sort of thing, broken chords rather, they had to spread the, spread the, spread the chords out and consequently, they started playing different kind of tunes. They, they, they, they, the way they, the way they tuned, the tunes were made up, it got away from where I used to play, uh, uh, Russian rag and maple, maple, maple, leaf, leaf, maple leaf rag and cataract and those things that like we used to play. We began to play, we began to play tunes like, uh, Swinging Down the Lane and, uh, Whispering and those tunes of course, and, and they were on a, just about a little different, different tempo and style. It has been very, uh, it has been very, uh, it has been something to, to notice, uh, the change of music, uh, change of music from, from the, the time the, the Dixieland, those fellas first brought that Dixieland out of New Orleans. They, uh, they, they, they, it has changed of course and I think one of the, one of the greatest, uh, one of the greatest changes that, uh, or one of, yes, one of the most revolutionary changes they made was when, uh, uh, after Don Redmond left the McKinney's Cotton Pickers and fixed his own, and took his own band. And he, you see, he, he was the first guy that, uh, first guy to really bring out the, uh, five, five saxophones and six brass, three trumpets and, and the three, or was it, yeah, three, three trumpets. And he's the first guy to write music, uh, with a double augment chord, uh, with that, uh, and his Chanted Weeds. Yeah, Chanted Weeds, you see, he, he's the guy that, uh, did that. And, of course, uh, since that time, why, uh, the music has been getting, uh, more complicated, if you would call it, uh, that is more complex. And that, uh, they're having these larger bands, uh, they had to find more places to put these, uh, play these, uh, instruments. And, of course, it brought on these, uh, sound like conflicting chords. Yeah. But it's, uh, it's another, it's another part of progress, of course. And, uh, you, you can never find, you can never stop that because it is always somebody trying something new. Yes.
